claims.text: The initial particles are equiatomic Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu solid-solution nanoparticles approximately 5–10 nm in diameter.
The synthesis route can produce initially homogeneous particles with minimal pre-existing segregation.
Copper has the lowest melting point among Fe, Ni, Cr, Co, and Cu.
At elevated temperature, copper atoms are more mobile than the other constituent atoms because of copper's lower melting temperature.
Copper preferentially diffuses to and segregates at the nanoparticle surface during heating.
Copper enrichment at the surface locally depresses the surface melting temperature.
A thin, liquid-like disordered surface layer forms before complete particle melting.
The particles consequently exhibit two-stage melting consisting of surface premelting followed by complete melting.
Differential elemental diffusivities and melting points govern the proposed two-stage melting process.
Diffusion rates differ among the constituent elements of chemically related Co–Cr–Cu–Fe–Mn–Ni high-entropy alloys.
Replacing copper with molybdenum replaces it with a higher-melting component.
Equiatomic Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu particles will begin surface disordering earlier than Cu-reduced or Cu-substituted particles.
Earlier surface disordering in the equiatomic particles will coincide with detectable copper enrichment at the surface.
Cu-reduced particles will exhibit less early surface premelting and a sharper melting transition closer to the bulk melting temperature.
The proposed mechanism is limited to approximately 5–10 nm Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles prepared with minimal initial segregation.
Size effects and synthesis-induced compositional inhomogeneity may dominate over copper segregation and thereby limit applicability of the mechanism.

Absence of both earlier surface disordering and surface copper enrichment relative to a Cu-reduced control, or persistence of the same premelting behavior after copper modification while size is controlled, would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The heating endpoint is described as above the bulk melting point but is also specified as roughly 0.8–1.1 times the melting temperature; the lower part of that interval is below, not above, the bulk melting point.
